techniques.name: Counterfactual Fairness Assessment
techniques.description: Counterfactual Fairness Assessment tests a model against the criterion of Kusner et al. (2017): a model is counterfactually fair if each individual's prediction would have had the same distribution had their protected attribute, such as race or sex, been different, with everything that attribute causes changed accordingly. The assessor first writes down a causal model, a graph of which variables cause which, covering the protected attribute, the model's inputs and unobserved background factors, and fits its equations to data. For each individual, the fitted model is used to infer the background factors from what was observed (abduction), set the protected attribute to another value (action) and recompute every input the attribute influences (prediction), giving a counterfactual version of that person. The model under test is run on the factual and counterfactual inputs, and the gap between the two predictions, per individual or as a distance between the two prediction distributions, is the evidence: distributions that lie on top of each other indicate counterfactual fairness under the assumed causal model. Every causal effect of the attribute counts as unfair, including effects that run through inputs it influences, such as test scores, which is what separates this criterion from versions that allow some pathways.

example_use_cases.description: A law school's admissions office uses a model to predict first-year grades from entrance-test scores and undergraduate grades. Its analysts build a causal model in which race and sex influence both inputs alongside an unobserved knowledge factor, fit it to past cohorts, and compare each applicant's predicted grade under actual and counterfactual race. A systematic shift shows that leaving race out of the inputs did not make the model counterfactually fair.

A credit risk team, working with economists, specifies a causal graph in which an applicant's ethnicity affects income and neighbourhood but not repayment behaviour directly, fits it to its applicant data, and checks whether the approval model's scores change for the counterfactual applicants. The result goes to the model risk committee together with the graph, because the conclusion holds only under that graph.

A public employment service reviewing a model that predicts job-seekers' risk of long-term unemployment from education and work history specifies, with labour-market researchers, how sex and migration background influence those inputs. It tests whether individual risk scores would change under counterfactual sex or migration background before the scores are used to allocate support.

limitations.description: The verdict rests on a causal model that cannot be checked against data: Kusner et al. note that counterfactual assumptions are generally unfalsifiable, even with experimental data, and should be treated as provisional. Different plausible graphs can give different verdicts, so a result is only as credible as the graph reported with it, and testing alternative graphs is part of the assessment.

A common cause left out of the graph, such as school quality affecting both test scores and later grades, biases the counterfactuals without any warning sign. Kilbertus et al. (2019) show that counterfactual fairness is sensitive to such unmeasured confounding and give tools to bound the effect for additive noise models, which adds a further analysis to do.

Every effect of the attribute counts as unfair, so a model that legitimately uses an input the attribute influences fails the test. Kusner et al. note that in practice few observed variables are unaffected by the attribute. Where some pathways are acceptable, for example where qualifications differ for reasons a decision may properly reflect, this criterion is stricter than the decision calls for.

Computing individual counterfactuals requires a fitted probabilistic model of the unobserved background factors; the original study fitted it in Stan, and DoWhy's counterfactual function needs mechanisms with additive noise and supports only continuous variables. With categorical inputs, many variables or unstructured data such as text and images, the assessment becomes hard to run or yields a spread of counterfactuals rather than one.

The counterfactual people are simulated by the fitted causal model, not observed. If its equations fit the data poorly or miss interactions, the counterfactual inputs are implausible and the measured gap reflects the causal model's errors as much as the predictor's; DoWhy's documentation notes counterfactual estimates are approximate for this reason.

resources.title: DoWhy: a Python library for causal inference (py-why/dowhy)
resources.abstract: DoWhy is a Python library for causal inference that supports explicit modeling and testing of causal assumptions. DoWhy is based on a unified language for causal inference, combining causal graphical models and potential outcomes frameworks.

resources.title: Counterfactual Fairness Evaluation of Machine Learning Models on Educational Datasets

sample_claims.text: Under the causal model agreed with the admissions committee, each applicant's predicted first-year grade has the same distribution under their actual and counterfactual race.
Under the documented causal graph linking ethnicity, income and neighbourhood, the credit model's approval scores do not change when applicants' ethnicity is counterfactually altered.

The unemployment-risk model's individual scores are unchanged under counterfactual sex and migration background, given the causal model reviewed by labour-market researchers, and the sensitivity of that result to unmeasured confounding has been bounded.

techniques.name: Path-Specific Counterfactual Fairness Assessment
techniques.description: A causal fairness evaluation technique that assesses algorithmic discrimination by examining specific causal pathways in a model's decision-making process. Unlike general counterfactual fairness, this approach enables practitioners to identify and intervene on particular causal paths that may introduce bias whilst preserving other legitimate pathways. The method uses causal graphs to distinguish between direct discrimination (through protected attributes) and indirect discrimination (through seemingly neutral factors that correlate with protected attributes), allowing for more nuanced fairness assessments in complex causal settings.

example_use_cases.description: Evaluating hiring algorithms by identifying which causal pathways from education and experience legitimately affect job performance versus those that introduce gender or racial bias, enabling targeted interventions that preserve merit-based selection whilst eliminating discriminatory pathways.

Analysing loan approval models to provide transparent evidence of which factors legitimately influence creditworthiness versus those that create indirect discrimination, enabling clear explanations to regulators about causal mechanisms underlying fair lending decisions.

limitations.description: Requires identifying which causal pathways are 'allowable' and which are not—a subjective decision; analyzing specific paths adds complexity to the causal model and the fairness criterion.

Causal graph construction relies on domain expertise and cannot be validated from observational data alone; if the graph incorrectly encodes causal structure or omits relevant edges, the path-specific assessment may certify an unfair model as compliant with no internal mechanism to detect the error, and this uncertainty is rarely surfaced in compliance documentation.

Path-specific causal effects are frequently non-identifiable from observational data alone; when unobserved confounders exist between a sensitive attribute and mediating variables or outcomes, the effect along a specific pathway cannot be uniquely recovered without additional parametric assumptions, reducing the technique to bounding rather than point-estimation of discrimination.
